reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / Endocrine Society
clinicalPearls: Symptoms range from reduced libido, erectile dysfunction, and infertility to fatigue, low mood, and loss of muscle mass and bone density
The core classification is primary (testicular) versus secondary (hypothalamic-pituitary) hypogonadism, guided by gonadotrophin levels
High LH and FSH with low testosterone indicate primary testicular failure, whereas low or inappropriately normal gonadotrophins indicate a central cause
Diagnosis requires a low morning total testosterone confirmed on a repeat sample, as levels have a diurnal rhythm and vary day to day
Interpretation should account for sex hormone-binding globulin, since altered SHBG can make total testosterone misleading and free testosterone more informative
Acute illness, obesity, sleep deprivation, and certain drugs transiently lower testosterone and should not be mistaken for true hypogonadism
Secondary hypogonadism warrants evaluation for pituitary disease, hyperprolactinaemia, and iron overload, with imaging when indicated
Testosterone replacement can relieve symptoms but suppresses spermatogenesis, so fertility goals must be addressed before starting therapy
reference.pathophysiology: Male hypogonadism is deficient testicular function affecting testosterone production, sperm production, or both. Primary hypogonadism arises from disease of the testes themselves, such as Klinefelter syndrome, cryptorchidism, orchitis, trauma, chemotherapy, or radiation, and is characterised by low testosterone with compensatory elevation of LH and FSH. Secondary (hypogonadotropic) hypogonadism arises from impaired hypothalamic or pituitary signalling, from congenital GnRH deficiency, pituitary tumours or infiltration, hyperprolactinaemia, haemochromatosis, or suppression by systemic illness and drugs, and shows low testosterone with low or inappropriately normal gonadotrophins. Testosterone deficiency reduces libido and sexual function, impairs spermatogenesis, and, if prolonged, decreases muscle mass, bone density, and erythropoiesis.
additionalDifferentials: Obesity and metabolic syndrome lowering SHBG and total testosterone
Functional suppression from acute or chronic illness
Erectile dysfunction of vascular, neurogenic, or psychogenic origin with normal testosterone
Depression or thyroid dysfunction mimicking symptoms
Opioid- or glucocorticoid-induced suppression of the axis
additionalInvestigations: Fasting morning total testosterone, repeated to confirm a low result
LH and FSH to classify primary versus secondary hypogonadism
SHBG with calculated or measured free testosterone when total levels are equivocal
Serum prolactin and iron studies in suspected secondary hypogonadism
Semen analysis when fertility is a concern
Karyotype for suspected Klinefelter syndrome and pituitary MRI for central causes
redFlags: Visual field defects or headache suggesting a pituitary or hypothalamic mass
Low testosterone with hyperprolactinaemia pointing to a prolactinoma
Features of haemochromatosis such as arthropathy, skin pigmentation, and diabetes
Very low testosterone with fragility fractures indicating significant bone loss
reference.prognosis: Outcomes depend on cause and reversibility; central hypogonadism from a treatable pituitary lesion or hyperprolactinaemia may recover, whereas primary testicular failure is usually permanent, and appropriate testosterone replacement improves symptoms, body composition, and bone health when fertility is not the immediate goal.
pitfalls: Diagnosing hypogonadism from a single non-fasting or afternoon testosterone sample
Ignoring SHBG effects so that total testosterone misrepresents androgen status
Starting testosterone in a man wishing to conceive, thereby suppressing sperm production
Overlooking a treatable central cause such as prolactinoma or iron overload
